title: The Jail Goes Global: 'Lock Upp' Trades MX Player for Netflix, and Now the Diaspora Gets a Cell Too
excerpt: Ektaa Kapoor's most unhinged reality experiment returns June 27 with Farah Khan and Riteish Deshmukh as jailers — and for the first time, NRIs can watch the chaos unfold the same night as Mumbai.
body:
The masked *qaidis* started appearing weeks ago. One slouched against a lamppost in Bandra. Another stood, hooded and silent, behind a set of prison bars bolted onto a billboard. By the time Netflix finally confirmed what everyone already suspected, the internet had done what it does best — turned an outdoor stunt into a guessing game. **Lock Upp** is back. And this time, it's not hiding behind a regional paywall.

Four years after **Kangana Ranaut** turned a prison-themed reality show into a 100-million-view phenomenon on MX Player and ALTBalaji, **Ektaa Kapoor's** badass jail reopens on **June 27, 2026** — exclusively on **Netflix**, streaming worldwide. New episodes drop Saturday through Wednesday at 8 PM IST, and the season runs a brutal six weeks, with a finale pencilled in for early August. The platform leap is the entire story here, and it's the kind of move that should make every NRI who has ever wrestled with a region-locked Indian app sit up.

https://x.com/NetflixIndia/status/2070447727344013801



> **"And there's the rare luxury of watching it *with* India, in real time, no VPN, no week-long lag, no "wait, don't spoil it." The qaidis are out of the regional cells and into the global yard."**


Because that's the thing about *Lock Upp* the first time around: if you lived in New Jersey or Slough or Brampton, you mostly experienced it through screenshots and Reddit recaps. MX Player and ALTBalaji were a maze for anyone outside India. Now the whole bloody saga lands on the same Netflix tile that's already on your TV, your phone, your hotel-room login. The diaspora doesn't get the highlight reel anymore. It gets the live feed.

The hosting chairs — sorry, *jailer* chairs — have changed hands, and the casting is inspired. Out goes Kangana, now a sitting Member of Parliament with rather different daily duties. In come **Farah Khan** and **Riteish Deshmukh**, arguably the most quietly lethal comic pairing on Indian television right now. Farah doesn't host so much as conduct interrogations with a smile; Riteish can disarm a contestant and then twist the knife in the same breath. Put them behind the warden's desk and you have two people who know exactly how to make a celebrity squirm on camera while making it look like affection.

> "The raw and real Yogesh that people connected with is exactly what they're going to see inside." — Yogesh Rawat, on entering the jail

The inmate roster is shaping up to be a glorious collision of worlds. TV royalty **Ram Kapoor** — forever the leading man of *Bade Achhe Lagte Hain* — walks in alongside *Yeh Rishta* favourite **Shivangi Joshi** and *Kundali Bhagya's* **Dheeraj Dhoopar**. Then there's the reality-TV bloodsport contingent: **Splitsvilla X6** alumni **Yogesh Rawat** and **Akanksha Choudhary**, who ended their last show on famously complicated terms and are now locked under one roof. Producer instinct, meet narrative dynamite. Rounding out the early reveals is **Desi Bling** star **Pamala Serena**, whose social-media fluency is precisely the sort of weapon this format rewards.

And in a piece of fan service that landed perfectly, Season 1 winner **Munawar Faruqui** broke *into* the new jail for a promo — joking that he and the prison simply can't quit each other — before pulling back the curtain on those first inmates. It was a wink to the original fanbase and a flex about how far the brand has travelled.

What makes *Lock Upp* worth the watch, even for skeptics, is that its rulebook is genuinely nasty in a way *Bigg Boss* has long stopped being. Fourteen inmates, a prison set, six weeks, and a single most-prized currency: the truth. Contestants earn basic necessities by completing tasks and by *confessing* — handing over secrets that can either shield them or detonate their entire game. Where *Bigg Boss* increasingly resembles a managed celebrity showcase, *Lock Upp* weaponises disclosure. The discomfort is the product.

For diaspora viewers, the appeal is double. There's the show itself — loud, messy, intoxicating in the way only a Balaji production can be. And there's the rare luxury of watching it *with* India, in real time, no VPN, no week-long lag, no "wait, don't spoil it." The qaidis are out of the regional cells and into the global yard. Grab a Netflix login and a strong cup of chai. The truth, apparently, is about to get expensive.
